title: Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. G.W. Thomas Drayage & Rigging Co.
summary: California’s contextual approach requires consideration of credible evidence that contract language bears the meaning a party proposes, even when the words initially seem clear.
notes: Chief Justice Traynor wrote the opinion (69 Cal.2d 33, 442 P.2d 641, decided July 11, 1968); the 1960 contract was for removing and replacing the upper cover of PG&E's steam turbine, and the trial court had excluded the extrinsic evidence on a 'plain meaning' rationale.

sections.Parties: Pacific Gas & Electric sought reimbursement from the contractor hired to remove and replace a turbine cover. The contractor appealed judgment under the agreement’s indemnity clause.
sections.Material Facts:
The contractor agreed to do the work at its own risk and expense and indemnify the utility against loss connected with injury to property arising from the work. It also had an insurance obligation, including coverage associated with the utility’s property. The turbine cover fell during the work and damaged the rotor; the utility sought $25,144.51 for repairs.

The contractor offered evidence from the utility’s agents, similar prior contracts, and other circumstances that the indemnity clause concerned third-party property only. The trial judge recognized that the clause resembled conventional third-party indemnity language but treated its words as plainly covering the utility’s own property and excluded the outside evidence.
sections.Procedural History: The utility dismissed its negligence count during trial and obtained judgment on the contract theory. The California Supreme Court reversed because the relevant extrinsic evidence was excluded. It did not finally find that the contractor’s proposed interpretation had been proved.
sections.Issue: Is evidence of contractual meaning admissible only after a court finds ambiguity on the face of the writing?
sections.Holding: No. The court must preliminarily consider credible evidence bearing on whether the language is reasonably susceptible to the proposed meaning. Evidence supporting such a meaning is then admissible to establish the interpretation.
sections.Reasoning:
Words take meaning from context, usage, purpose, and the circumstances of their use. A judge’s initial reading reflects the judge’s own linguistic experience and need not be the parties’ intended meaning. A writing’s apparent clarity therefore cannot alone justify refusing all evidence about the meaning the parties attached to it.

The approach still limits interpretation. The offered meaning must be one the language can reasonably bear; the opinion does not authorize adding any desired obligation under the label of interpretation. The court must identify the terms before deciding that evidence would improperly vary them.

Here the contractor’s proposed third-party meaning was reasonably possible and the evidence was relevant to it. The opinion also noted an independent point: the recognized double use of indemnity language made exclusion questionable even under the more restrictive facial-ambiguity approach. Admission of evidence and ultimate acceptance of an interpretation remain separate steps.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It provides the contextual side of the course’s comparison with New York’s more restrictive treatment of extrinsic evidence.

topics.interpretation: Credible context can expose a reasonable meaning that is not apparent from the text alone.
topics.assent: Interpretation seeks the meaning expressed by these parties in context.
topics.parol-evidence: The meaning of the written terms must be identified before deciding whether evidence impermissibly varies them.
topics.governing-law: The case supplies California law later applied, despite criticism, by federal courts.
topics.integration: Traynor's contextual approach governs how extrinsic evidence is used even against an apparently integrated and unambiguous writing.
topics.objective-assent: The opinion rejects the idea that words carry fixed meanings independent of the parties' shared understanding, bearing on how objective assent is determined.

mnemonic.rationale: A turbine cover and an indemnity clause
